extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political theory and constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative standards for designing and judging constitutions and regimes, emphasizing mixed government (monarchy/aristocracy/democracy), separation of powers, property balance, representation, and judicial safeguards, illustrated with historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed composition (monarchy, aristocracy, democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The best governments have been composed of the three simple species — monarchy, aristocracy, and democracy — and receive praise or blame according as these parts are well or ill proportioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a constitution includes elements of the three forms and whether the dominant part is properly tempered by the others. Examples: Sparta (two kings, senate, assemblies), Rome (king/consuls, senate, people), Venice (duke, senate, great assembly). Anti-pattern: labeling a mixed regime simply 'democracy' when it is composed of three parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation into three powers
rubrics_metrics.description: In every government there are three sorts of power: the legislative, the executive (in respect of the law of nations and general security), and the judicial (executive regarding civil law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether these powers are separately defined and allocated. The clear doctrinal split (legislative / executive / judiciary) is a baseline metric for constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and executive must not be united
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person or body, there can be no liberty because that body could enact tyrannical laws and execute them tyrannically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check institutional arrangements to ensure the legislature cannot both make and unilaterally execute laws. Anti-pattern: single body with lawmaking and enforcement authority leading to arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from legislature and executive
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no liberty if the power of judging is not separated from the legislative and executive powers; joined with either it exposes life and liberty to arbitrary control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether judges are institutionally and functionally independent of lawmakers and executors. Look for safeguards (tenure, appointment processes, budgetary independence) and historical examples where unity led to oppression (e.g., some Italian republics, Turkish sultan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judiciary should be drawn from the people and temporary where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The judiciary ought not to be a standing senate; it should be exercised by persons taken from the body of the people, at certain times and pursuant to law, erecting tribunals that last only as long as necessity requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score whether judicial bodies are permanent professional elites or whether there are institutions (jury pools, temporary tribunals, citizen magistrates) that diffuse judging power among citizens. Benefit: judges become 'invisible' and office is feared, not the person. Anti-pattern: a closed caste of magistrates dominating all tribunals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgments must conform to the exact letter of the law
rubrics_metrics.description: Though tribunals need not be fixed, their judgments ought to be always conformable to the exact letter of the law; judges must not substitute private opinion for law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal certainty and predictability: presence of codified laws, constraints on judicial discretion, and mechanisms to prevent arbitrary interpretation. Anti-pattern: judges ruling according to private opinion causing unpredictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of the accused to challenge or partly choose judges in serious cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In accusations of a deep or criminal nature, the accused should have the privilege of choosing, in some measure, his judges, or at least the right to except against so great a number that the remaining part may be deemed his own choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine procedural protections for defendants: voir dire, challenge mechanisms, impartial panel selection. Absence of such rights indicates weaker procedural fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature ideally resides in the whole people but practically in representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: In a free state the legislative power should reside in the whole body of the people, but since this is impossible in large states it is fit the people should execute by their representatives what they cannot execute themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representative institutions: are representatives elected by local constituencies? Do they meaningfully reflect popular will? Anti-pattern: remote or appointed bodies that do not answer to local electorates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives should be capable of deliberation and not micromanaged
rubrics_metrics.description: The great advantage of representatives is their capacity for discussing affairs; they should not wait to be particularly instructed on every affair, which would cause delays and allow individual deputies to control assemblies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score the autonomy and deliberative capacity of legislators: presence of mandate/independence vs. strict imperative mandates from constituencies (e.g., German diets). Too much binding instruction hampers timely decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative selection from local constituencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the legislature should be chosen from the general body of the nation but it is proper that in every considerable place a representative should be elected by the inhabitants, since they best know their own wants and the capacity of neighbors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for district-based representation and local accountability. Anti-pattern: at-large systems or appointments that disconnect representatives from local knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure democracy fits only very small communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure democracy can suit only the convenience of a small town accompanied by rare circumstances; in large states pure democracy is impractical and often problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess size and complexity of polity when judging feasibility of direct-democratic institutions. Use caution in applying direct rule mechanisms to large polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of dominion/property determines form and stability of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The balance of dominion (property, especially land) among one, a few, or many hands is the natural cause of empire; proportions of property determine whether a state tends to monarchy, mixed monarchy, or commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate property distribution as a structural variable: concentration favors monarchy/oligarchy, broad ownership favors commonwealth. Historical guidance: Harrington and Aristotle—imbalances lead to sedition or regime change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixing land balance (agrarian laws) can stabilize regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws fixing the balance of land (agrarian laws) — limiting alienation or prescribing distributions — can render the balance immovable and thus stabilize a constitution (example: Lycurgus's laws in Sparta).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for institutional land/wealth rules that prevent excessive concentration (inheritance rules, alienation statutes). Such policies are a tool for long-term regime stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia/public sword depends on property balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The public sword (militia) is inseparable from the over-balance in dominion; an army must be fed and its maintenance depends on pastures (resources), which in turn ties military power to property distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess relationship between military power and property structure: whether militias are citizen-based (linked to property) or standing professional armies beholden to rulers. Anti-pattern: standing armies maintained by the state that erode civic control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentration of powers in magistracy of one class reduces liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: When different tribunals (legislative, executive, judiciary) are composed of magistrates all belonging to the same body (e.g., the same nobility), they constitute almost one and the same power, diminishing liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether institutional design trades plurality of estates for a single class's dominance. Anti-pattern: hereditary aristocratic republics where all key offices are held by the same social group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary emergency powers must be limited and legislatively authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislature may authorize the executive for a short and limited time to imprison suspected persons if it believes itself in danger (e.g., secret conspiracy), but otherwise giving the executive a right to imprison those who can give security ends liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check existence, scope, and time limits of emergency detention powers and legislative oversight. Anti-pattern: open-ended executive detention without speedy trial or legislative limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate share of the three estates supports stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the three estates (royalty, aristocracy, commons) should retain its proper share in government; when their authority is duly proportioned and mixed it gives the highest degree of perfection a commonwealth can attain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess power-sharing mechanisms and institutional checks that ensure no estate wholly subsumes the others. Historical example: creation of tribunes in Rome to give plebeians a share.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspecting officers and assemblies to restrain monarchic power
rubrics_metrics.description: Some systems keep royal dignity hereditary but restrain power by instituting officers or assemblies (e.g., Ephori, Maire du Palais, justiciar) to inspect proceedings of rulers and ensure laws are not violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether constitutional offices exist to monitor executive/monarchical action; such offices are evaluated as anti-concentration measures and accountability mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban vs. rural composition affects political character
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealths rooted in country/tillage (owners of the plow) tend to produce steadier, more libertarian citizens, whereas those dominated by city life and commerce are more prone to ambition and instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider socio-economic composition (agrarian vs. urban/trade) as a factor in regime durability and political culture; a polity's social base should be part of constitutional assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid micromanagement of representatives by imperative mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring representatives to be particularly instructed on every affair (as in some diets) causes delays and gives each deputy a power of controlling the assembly, impeding urgent action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether electoral/constitutional rules bind representatives in ways that create paralysis; favor frameworks that grant deliberative latitude while preserving accountability.
